papers.title: Agentic Distributional Regression: Conditional Density Estimation through Agent-Written Programs
papers.abstract: In this paper we propose a method for estimating conditional densities from an iid sample using a language-model agent. The agent writes the estimator as a short program that, for each covariate value, returns the estimated conditional distribution of the response. The program is built from a library of probability distributions, so the returned law can be a parametric distribution, a mixture or a multivariate factorization, with parameters given by explicit functions of the covariates. Since the number of operations and constants in the program is limited, the fitted conditional density is a formula that can be inspected and evaluated independently of the agent, while the choice of the model structure and of the fitting procedure is left to the agent. We call this approach agentic distributional regression (ADR). Treating the returned program as a random conditional density estimator, we derive a finite-sample error bound under explicit complexity and optimization assumptions, and an oracle inequality for selection using independent validation data. For a stably selected regular structure with sufficiently accurate fitting, we obtain asymptotic normality of the fitted constants. In simulation studies, on twelve real datasets and on a new dataset collected after the agents' training data, ADR with Claude Opus 5.5 has the best average performance among the methods considered.

papers.title: A flexible approach to high-dimensional clustering and classification using mixtures of finite mutually repulsive mixtures
papers.abstract: We propose a novel approach for clustering that is later extended to classification. Our methods are based on an underlying determinantal point process (DPP) that generates sparsity and separation of location parameters in a mixture of finite mixture models specification. A key aspect is the assumption of a DPP conditional on the number of groups and a prior on this number, which results in a dynamic mixture of repulsive mixtures. The proposed model also involves a sparse tensor decomposition of the covariance function used to define the DPP, which is coupled with a separate mixture model employed to handle the intra-cluster correlation structure. Further computational enhancement in the high-dimensional case comes from exploiting a mapping from Euclidean space to the space of (valid) correlation matrices. A suitable posterior simulation scheme involving a modified telescopic sampler is developed. The resulting approach is seen to perform satisfactorily in simulated and real data examples.

papers.title: Practical Guidelines for Goodness-of-Fit Testing for Right-Censored Data
papers.abstract: In survival studies, right censoring often prevents the observation of subjects' complete outcomes, complicating inference about the underlying distribution. Evaluating whether a given distribution adequately fits right-censored data is therefore essential. However, guidance on the relative performance of available goodness-of-fit tests under different data conditions remains limited. In this work, we present a comparative assessment of three classical goodness-of-fit tests adapted for right-censored data: Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Anderson-Darling, and Cramér-von Mises. Through an extensive simulation study, we investigate how factors such as the proportion of right-censored observations, sample size, and distributional symmetry influence the statistical power of each test. All procedures were implemented using the R package GofCens, and power estimates were obtained from extensive replicated simulations. The results identify the settings in which each test exhibits superior performance, providing practical, evidence-based recommendations for test selection in survival analysis. These recommendations are summarized as user-oriented guidelines and complemented by a concise graphical cheat sheet, enabling practitioners to quickly identify the most suitable test for their specific application.

papers.title: Contemporaneous Transmission Networks and Systemic Risk in European Banking
papers.abstract: We study how contemporaneous equity-return transmission shapes systemic exposure among 51 listed European banks. Using a recursive non-Gaussian network model on volatility-standardized returns, we construct two market-capitalization-weighted measures based on direct and indirect transmission effects: the Systemic Impact Score (SIS), capturing a bank's potential influence on other institutions, and the Systemic Vulnerability Score (SVS), capturing its exposure to disturbances originating elsewhere. The fitted network reveals distinct transmitting and receiving roles, highlighting differences between institutions with substantial outward influence and those with high incoming sensitivity. Receiving roles are generally more reproducible than transmitting roles across repeated network discovery, and selected connections remain informative about lower-tail dependence in subsequent observations. Volatility standardization substantially reduces detected dependence among recovered shocks, although the full-sample model does not satisfy the designated criterion for supporting shock independence. Alternative recursive orderings also yield comparable directional tail asymmetries, limiting the extent to which these patterns validate a particular ordering. The results provide complementary measures of model-implied systemic transmission and vulnerability, with explicit attention to uncertainty and identification limits

papers.title: HGPRGDel: GPR-Aware Learning and Ranking for Growth-Coupled Gene Deletion Design
papers.abstract: Designing microbial strains for growth-coupled production, in which cellular growth is linked to the synthesis of a target compound through genetic interventions, is a fundamental goal in metabolic engineering. Constraint-based methods can identify growth-coupled deletion strategies, but design for each target typically requires a separate search across a large number of possible gene-deletion combinations. This motivates a reusable approach that learns from previously evaluated strain designs to prioritize candidate interventions before downstream constraint-based evaluation. We present a reproducible protocol for growth-coupled gene deletion design that learns and ranks gene-deletion priorities for each target metabolite. Using computationally curated deletion strategies as learning resources, the protocol generates continuous deletion-priority rankings, constructs candidate strategies at adjustable search-space budgets, and evaluates these candidates through constraint-based metabolic analysis. Its learning component, HGPRGDel, explicitly represents gene-protein-reaction (GPR) logic, capturing how multiple genes can jointly support a reaction or alternative genes can maintain its activity, while integrating molecular and reaction-level information. Across e_coli_core, iMM904, and iML1515, the protocol achieves the highest macro-F1 and AUC among the evaluated learning configurations. HGPRGDel's rankings recovered an average of 90% of the reference deletion genes from MetNetComp by examining fewer genes than the evaluated baseline methods. By separating learned intervention prioritization from downstream constraint-based assessment, the protocol provides a reproducible framework for reusing strain-design knowledge while controlling the size of the candidate space and retaining mechanistic evaluation of growth-coupled production.

papers.title: Bayesian Ordinal Analysis of Cereal Growth Stage Data from Oat Trials in Western Australia
papers.abstract: Growth stage in cereal field trials is usually scored on the Zadoks decimal scale. The score is ordinal, yet it is often analysed as if it were continuous, which can lead to misleading conclusions. Ordinal analysis of growth stage data has received little attention from biometricians or agronomists, and it is not straightforward when several plants are scored in each plot of a split-plot design. We analysed Zadoks scores recorded four weeks after sowing on ten plants per plot in two deep-sowing oat trials in Western Australia, using a Bayesian hierarchical ordinal model that carries the full split-plot structure and an AR1 x AR1 spatial covariance. The implementation was validated on simulated data, and the candidate models were compared by five-fold cross-validation over plots. Adding a random effect at the experimental-unit (plot) level changed the uncertainty of the sub-plot contrasts substantially, while the main-plot contrasts changed little. How that plot-level heterogeneity was modelled mattered much less. At either site, cross-validation could not separate the candidate models that carried a plot-level term, whether or not they included an AR1 x AR1 field or the blocking terms, and the autoregressive parameters were only weakly identified on this layout. Deeper sowing (80 and 120 mm against 30 mm) went with more advanced development at four weeks in both trials. Sowing at 120 mm rather than 30 mm raised the predicted probability of tillering from 0.04 to 0.24 at Wickepin and from 0.04 to 0.10 at Merredin. The depth effects were stable whether or not the spatial field was fitted, and under both the cumulative and the sequential ordinal family.

papers.title: Cost-based variable selection for prediction models
papers.abstract: Objective: Variable selection for clinical prediction models is commonly done on statistical grounds related to model fit. Statistical approaches ignore the cost of misclassifications and the harm of measuring a variable. We aim to develop a decision-analytic variable selection algorithm based on net benefit. Materials and Methods: The proposed algorithm selects the set of predictors by exhaustively comparing the net benefit of all combinations using cross validation, with an extension based on backward elimination for settings with many predictors. Variables are selected if the increased net benefit from better predictiveness exceeds the net benefit reduction from the harm of variable measurement. Harm includes financial expense, time, resource allocation, and patient burden. We illustrate the algorithm through a simulated example and three real case studies. We compare its performance to traditional backward elimination and LASSO. Results: Across the case studies, parsimonious models were generated that optimized clinical utility with minimal impact on discrimination and calibration. Penalizing predictors based on their cost ensured that expensive or burdensome variables were only selected if they offer sufficient clinical utility. The algorithm was implemented in the R package NBvarsel. Discussion: Decision-analytic variable selection allows prediction models to maximize patient benefit while minimizing unnecessary clinical burden and costs. Conclusion: Clinical utility should not be an afterthought reserved only for implementation. By integrating a harm-adjusted net benefit metric directly into the variable selection process, NBvarsel allows researchers to select only the variables that sufficiently improve clinical utility.

papers.title: Personal preference or system role? Battery swapping among UK electric vehicle users
papers.abstract: Battery swapping replaces a depleted EV battery with a charged one, reducing waiting time and enabling off-peak charging. Evidence on acceptance, however, remains concentrated in Asian markets, and most studies examine individual adoption intentions. This study asks whether current UK EV users judge swapping differently as a purchase option and as a technology for the transport system. Using Behavioural Reasoning Theory, an integrated choice and latent variable model, and latent class analysis, we analyse perceived usefulness, energy-system concerns, practical barriers, and satisfaction with current charging. Usefulness and energy-system concerns relate more strongly to expectations about the system. Battery compatibility and station coverage relate more strongly to personal preference, while spare battery costs relate to expectations about network viability. User groups differ in how they balance benefits, barriers, and satisfaction with existing charging. Policy should address driver barriers and network viability as distinct but connected priorities.

papers.title: Penalized Cause-Specific Hazard Regression under Competing Risks: An Elastic Net Approach Using SANAD Trial Data
papers.abstract: Competing risks analysis is an important framework for studying time-to-event data in the presence of multiple, mutually exclusive events. Traditional methods, such as non-parametric estimators and proportional hazards models, may not adequately capture complex hazard patterns or provide stable estimates in practical settings. In this study, we propose a parametric approach based on the generalized exponential regression model for competing risks data. The model allows flexible hazard shapes and incorporates covariate effects through a regression structure. To improve estimation stability, we integrate elastic net regularization into the likelihood framework. The proposed method is evaluated through simulation studies and applied to a real dataset. The results indicate that the elastic net approach provides more stable and precise estimates compared to standard maximum likelihood estimation. Overall, the proposed framework offers a flexible and practical approach for analyzing competing risks data.

papers.title: Efficient Bootstrap Calibration of Generalized Posteriors with Importance Reweighting
papers.abstract: The learning rate of a generalized posterior governs posterior uncertainty but typically has no canonical value. Generalized posterior calibration (GPC) selects this rate by matching bootstrap-estimated credible-interval coverage to its nominal level, often requiring repeated posterior simulation. We propose GPC via importance reweighting (GPC-IRW), which reuses draws from a reference posterior fitted to the original data across bootstrap resamples and candidate learning rates. For quantile-based intervals of a scalar functional, we express the coverage criterion in terms of bootstrap posterior cumulative distribution functions, avoiding computation of individual bootstrap credible intervals. Safeguards based on importance-weight effective sample size and proximity to coverage-decision boundaries invoke reweighting from cached bootstrap-specific draws or direct posterior simulation when necessary. Under the stated regularity conditions, with numerical error tending to zero, we show that median-centered calibration preserves the first-order learning-rate target and achieves asymptotically nominal coverage. The approach extends to independent clusters through cluster-level resampling. Simulations yield coverage and interval lengths comparable to those of existing GPC algorithms at substantially lower computational cost. In an exoplanet mass-radius analysis, GPC-IRW achieves 6.7- and 9.6-fold speedups over MCMC-based calibration in the single-planet and full-sample analyses, respectively, while illustrating the effects of within-host dependence.

papers.title: Estimation and Inference for One-pass Streaming Function-on-Function Regression
papers.abstract: In many applications, functional pairs are collected sequentially from a data stream. Existing function-on-function regression methods are primarily designed for batch data, and bootstrap inference has become one of the most popular approaches. However, this procedure may be infeasible when observations cannot be stored. In this paper, we propose a one-pass functional SGD estimator that updates upon each observation's arrival without data storage, and a weighted rolling validation rule is provided for step size selection for implementation. Further, an online multiplier bootstrap is developed for inference that updates perturbed stochastic gradient paths in parallel, bypassing estimating an infinite-dimensional covariance operator. Asymptotic behaviors are established for the proposed method, and conditional bootstrap validity is justified for the bias-centered pointwise estimation error. Simulation studies and two real data applications confirm the empirical effectiveness of the proposed procedures. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first theoretically justified one-pass framework for bootstrap inference on a bivariate coefficient surface with streaming functional data.

papers.title: An Application of Geometric Riemannian Pricing Algorithm for Valuing Catastrophe Bonds in Incomplete Markets: Market-Consistent Financial Entropy and the Split of Frequency and Severity Risk Premia
papers.abstract: This paper presents a framework for pricing catastrophe (CAT) bonds in incomplete markets through Riemannian geometric optimization of financial entropy. We formulate pricing-measure selection as a maximum financial entropy problem on a finite-dimensional manifold of equivalent measures, parameterized by the non-hedgeable market prices of catastrophe frequency and severity risk, with discounting fixed by the default-free term structure. Since unconstrained entropy maximization recovers the physical measure, we incorporate observed secondary-market spreads, both pooled and date by date. For a compound Poisson-generalized Pareto loss model with Wang distortion, we derive closed-form expressions for financial entropy and the Riemannian metric. We show that CAT bond prices depend on frequency and severity premia primarily through the risk-neutral trigger intensity, making the two premia unidentifiable from market data alone; the entropy criterion resolves this ambiguity. Using a hypothetical earthquake CAT bond calibrated to quarterly spreads of Golden State Re II Ltd. (Series 2014-1), we obtain risk-neutral trigger intensities of 6.58 to 10.45 times the physical intensity (9.20 pooled and 18.26 at the end of 2015). The model-implied risk multiple aligns with the market spread-to-expected-loss ratio (8.87 versus 8.81 at issuance). The minimal-entropy measure attributes 53.5% to 63.7% of the log risk multiple to frequency risk, reflecting the selection principle rather than market identification. Finally, equating the coupon with the quoted spread understates the risk multiple by approximately half.

papers.title: Is Your LLM Relay Serving What It Claims? A low-cost and high-power test for LLM Relay Auditing
papers.abstract: Relay and reseller APIs have become a common way to access large language models (LLMs), yet users cannot directly verify whether they receive the models they request and pay for. This opacity motivates LLM relay auditing, but existing methods struggle to combine low cost, robustness to benign deployment changes, and statistically interpretable decisions under black-box access. To address these limitations, we propose distributional fingerprint auditing (DFA), a statistical method that requires only textual responses from suspect and trusted reference endpoints. DFA repeatedly queries semantically simple finite-choice probes and uses the resulting categorical response distributions to construct endpoint fingerprints. It compares the suspect and reference fingerprints probe by probe and aggregates the resulting evidence using the Cauchy combination test, yielding an approximate endpoint-level $p$-value for audit decisions at a prespecified nominal significance level. Using registered fingerprints of candidate models, a likelihood-based formulation further supports model attribution under full substitution and joint estimation of substitute identity and substitution ratio under constant-ratio mixed routing. Our benchmark includes 16 proprietary and open-weight LLMs from 10 model families. Across 240 ordered full-substitution pairs, DFA achieves high detection rates at a nominal significance level of $α=0.05$, using five probes and 250 relay requests per audit with stored reference fingerprints. Configuration overrides can lead to rejection even when the served model remains unchanged, with effects varying across models and configurations. Simulations based on stored empirical fingerprints demonstrate accurate model attribution and estimate substitution ratios, with estimation error decreasing as the audit budget increases.

papers.title: Reducing Complexity of Pseudo-Marginal Sequential Monte Carlo via Hierarchical Tempering
papers.abstract: The Bayesian approach to inverse problems provides a powerful framework for inferring unknown parameters from noisy observations. Among the computationally most challenging statistical inference problems are problems with intractable likelihoods, especially if no unbiased likelihood estimator is available. We focus on a class of such problems, where a biased likelihood estimator is obtained through a stochastic approximation of a forward map (stochastic solver). Obtaining an empirical posterior approximation in applications is very expensive due to the repeated stochastic solver evaluations required by standard sampling methods. To address this computational bottleneck, we develop a novel algorithm based on a density-tempered marginalized Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) sampler. Our approach (hierarchical SMC) accelerates inference by leveraging a hierarchy of stochastic solvers with increasing accuracy both along the tempering sequence and within mutation stages of the SMC sampler. We establish, under additional assumptions, that the asymptotic speedup is proportional to the number of tempering stages $T$. We demonstrate computational gains on several examples, including a nonlinear, high-contrast inverse problem arising in photoacoustic medical imaging. On this problem, we demonstrate a speedup by a factor of 14.3, reducing the inference wall-clock time from about 4.6 days to 7.7 hours on an NVIDIA A40 GPU.

papers.title: Analysis of Uncertain GARCH Model with the application of crude oil future prices
papers.abstract: Time series data often exhibit variation, clustering, and persistence in uncertain environments. Based on an uncertain measure, existing studies have primarily focused on conditional mean structures while ignoring variance and persistent dynamics. To address this gap, this paper develops an uncertain generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (UGARCH) model that incorporates lagged conditional variance terms. We first prove sufficient conditions to ensure mean stationarity of the variance process. Then, we propose recursive constrained least squares to estimate the model parameters and use cross validation to determine the orders of the mean and variance equations. In addition, we also employ uncertain hypothesis tests to determine whether a time series exhibits a UGARCH effect and to assess the goodness of fit. Point and interval forecasts are subsequently constructed from the recursively obtained next-period conditional variance and the expected value of the mean equation. Numerical simulations demonstrate the parameter estimation performance of the proposed method and show that UGARCH achieves smaller conditional-variance fitting errors than UARCH under the considered settings. In the empirical analysis, we apply the proposed method to West Texas Intermediate crude oil futures closing prices, which exhibit time-varying volatility and support short-term point and interval forecasts. Keywords: Uncertain measure, Uncertain time-series analysis, UGARCH model, hypothesis test

papers.title: Identifying and disentangling direct and spillover effects using multiple pre-treatment periods
papers.abstract: Under interference, the treatment of some units affects the outcomes of others, so that the effect on a treated unit consists of a direct and a spillover component. A non-treated comparison group then generally identifies neither component, but the difference between the total effect on the treated and the spillover effect on the comparison units. We show that both components are identified separately when multiple pre-treatment periods are available, without an uncontaminated comparison group. Under no anticipation, pre-treatment outcomes are free of both components for every unit. Extrapolating the pre-treatment trend within a group, as in interrupted time series approaches, therefore identifies the counterfactual outcome in the absence of any treatment. Applied to the treated it gives the total effect on them, applied to the non-treated at a given level of exposure the spillover effect on them. Disentangling the two components in addition requires effect homogeneity across treated and non-treated units with the same exposure and covariates, as well as common support in exposure. We derive doubly robust and Neyman-orthogonal expressions for the effects of interest, which permits controlling for covariates by machine learning, and establish asymptotic normality. A simulation study confirms the root-$n$ behaviour of the estimators and the reliability of the standard errors. We apply the framework to the compulsory licensing of enemy-owned patents in the United States in 1919. Licensing raised patenting in the licensed subclasses and in technologically close ones alike, so that a comparison-group design understates the total effect.

papers.title: pyTransRate: 1 reference-free quality assessment of de novo transcriptome assemblies with current aligners and quantifiers
papers.abstract: Summary: The original software TransRate scores a de novo transcriptome assembly by mapping the reads it was built from back to it, with no reference required. Its last release (1.0.3) depends on Ruby 2.2 and on aligner and quantifier versions that can no longer be installed on most systems. pyTransRate is a Python reimplementation of the TransRate method built on snap-aligner 2.0.5 and salmon 2.7.0. In 5,031 paired comparisons (39 assembly-level metrics on each of 129 public assemblies), it reproduces the original sequence metrics and read counts exactly and ranks assemblies consistently with 1.0.3 (Spearman rho = 0.94 for assembly score, 0.98 for good-mapping rate), although its read-based scores are not numerically interchangeable with the original. It also reads gzip- and bgzip-compressed input directly. Availability and Implementation: pyTransRate is implemented in Python 3 and is freely available under the MIT license at https://github.com/macmanes-lab/pytransrate. It runs on Linux and macOS; snap-aligner and salmon are installed from Bioconda. Supplementary information: Supplementary data are available online. Supplementary Table S1 lists the assembly and read accessions for every assembly analyzed; Supplementary Table S2 gives per-assembly values from both implementations.

papers.title: Dynamic Properties of Numerical Solution for Stochastic Epidemic Models with a Fully Implicit Form
papers.abstract: This paper establishes a fully implicit model to investigate the spread of epidemics and studies its dynamic properties, extending the semi-implicit model in Yang et al.(Commun. Nonlinear Sci. Numer. Simul., 152 (2026) 109140 ). We first employ the split-step backward Euler method to address the non-adaptability arising from backward Euler discretization and ensure the global convergence of the numerical solution. By linearizing the model, the computational cost is reduced at the expense of a slight increase in error, effectively avoiding complex iterative solution processes. Then, we derive the existence, uniqueness, positivity, and boundedness of the numerical solution, and obtain its global convergence order. On this basis, the extinction and persistence of the disease are investigated under three different scenarios. The results indicate that environmental noise is a key factor leading to disease extinction. Finally, numerical simulations visually verify the obtained theoretical conclusions.

papers.title: Neural Simulation-Based Inference for space-time Gaussian processes
papers.abstract: In spatio-temporal data analysis, estimating covariance parameters for Gaussian random fields via maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) is computationally prohibitive for large datasets. Following recent advances in simulation-based inference techniques, we propose two neural network architectures - Neural Bayes Estimation (NBE) and Neural Ratio Estimation (NRE) - to learn the parameters of Gaussian spatio-temporal Gneiting-Mat{é}rn models with advection. The networks are trained on simulations generated directly from the underlying Gaussian random field model. A thorough simulation study demonstrates strong performance across one-dimensional time and both one-dimensional space and two-dimensional space, yielding high accuracy and reliable uncertainty quantification for both NBE and NRE. Through extensive offline training, the framework achieves fully amortized inference, replacing costly optimization with a single forward pass. Finally, we apply our framework to solar radiation prediction and short-term forecasting. By adopting a sliding-window approach, the model accounts for temporal non-stationarity while retaining this key advantage: achieving near-instantaneous parameter inference and forecasting.

papers.title: Joint Distributional Copula Regression for Insurance Claim Frequency and Severity via Boosting
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose a model-based boosting approach for fitting structured additive distributional copula regression models with bivariate responses, focusing particularly on the joint modeling of claim frequency and claim severity. The proposed approach is based on generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSS), which extend the general idea of GAMs by allowing multiple parameters of a response distribution, rather than only its conditional mean, to depend on covariates. The model is therefore intrinsically interpretable at the level of its additive predictors, providing greater transparency and auditability than black-box alternatives. We evaluate the proposed framework using synthetic and real-world data. We demonstrate its ability to recover the underlying covariate effects and dependence structure, identify informative variables, and achieve competitive predictive performance relative to benchmark models. We also illustrate how the fitted model can be interpreted.

papers.title: LLM knowledge for improved Out-of-Distribution Tabular Prediction - A Cross-Validated Regularisation Approach
papers.abstract: Prediction models degrade when the deployment population differs from the one used to train them, and training data cannot say which feature-response relationships will transfer. Expert elicitation is slow and unscalable. We ask whether coefficient priors elicited from large language models (LLMs) improve out-of-distribution (OOD) prediction as the shrinkage target of a regularised regression instead of zero, across five tabular datasets split on real covariates, selecting providers and prior structures by source-domain cross-validation alone. The priors help on four of five datasets, by up to 7.9% OOD mean squared error, and ten of twenty-four prior-informed results resolve the mean improvement at conventional confidence; single-deployment intervals are much wider. On classification the gain is in probabilistic accuracy, not ranking, and control tests with corrupted priors attribute the benefit to feature-specific content rather than scale. Two findings temper this. Variation across candidate priors exceeds the average benefit, yet cross-validation margins fall below their own noise, so selection avoids the worst prior rather than finding the best. On three datasets the prior improves in-domain accuracy as much as out-of-domain, making it better regularisation than shift correction. Only where the training data are large enough that the in-domain gain disappears does elicited knowledge demonstrably improve transfer. Code, priors and results: https://github.com/hugohammer/llm-priors-ood.

papers.title: A Semiparametric Real-Time GARCH Model with Nonstationary Variance
papers.abstract: We propose a semiparametric real-time GARCH (SRT-GARCH) model that combines a smooth deterministic long-run volatility component with a stationary short-run process driven by contemporaneous return innovations. The model accommodates gradual changes in unconditional variance while allowing short-run volatility to respond directly to current information rather than relying solely on lagged observations. We derive the variance normalization, conditional moments, and closed-form conditional density of the model. For estimation, we develop a two-step procedure that combines kernel smoothing with conditional Gaussian maximum likelihood. Under Gaussian innovations and mild regularity conditions, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the short-run parameter estimator. The analysis exploits geometric moment contraction to control serial dependence and shows that estimating the long-run component adds a positive semidefinite rank-one adjustment to the oracle covariance matrix obtained when the long-run component is known. The resulting asymptotic covariance matrix admits a plug-in estimator that requires neither lag truncation nor additional tuning parameters. Monte Carlo simulations show good finite-sample performance of the estimator and the associated inference procedure. Applications to FTSE~100 returns and U.S. natural gas futures show that allowing for a time-varying long-run component improves forecasting relative to the parametric RT-GARCH benchmark, while the additional real-time feedback mechanism provides more pronounced gains in the natural gas application than in the FTSE application. The proposed model also delivers competitive one-step-ahead Value-at-Risk forecasts.

papers.title: Bias-Aware Guardrail Selection Under Network Interference
papers.abstract: Web platforms use randomized experiment logs to choose budget-feasible treatment allocations while limiting losses to a designated group of units. Under network interference, each allocation requires expected outcomes at treatment-exposure pairs that may be sparsely observed. Existing safe policy selection methods require valid inference for each candidate, but pooling nearby exposures to improve estimability can introduce allocation-specific bias that variance-only bounds omit. We propose exposure-stratified guardrail selection (ESGuard), which aggregates unit-level bias bounds into a bias bound on each candidate's guardrail effect. It incorporates these bounds into simultaneous lower confidence bounds to select an allocation or retain the status quo. Under randomized rounds, a correct exposure mapping, and valid curvature and slope bounds, the conditional bias bound holds in finite samples. With independent rounds and additional regularity conditions, the unconditional probability of selecting an unsafe allocation is asymptotically at most the target level. We evaluate ESGuard on a simulator built from New York City ride-hailing trips. With six months of simulated rounds, we compare estimators that pool nearby exposures on the same logs and candidate sets. Adding the bias bound raises simultaneous coverage from below the nominal 95 percent level to at least 95 percent for every estimator in this comparison. In the underserved-only scenario, ESGuard violates the guardrail in 0.06 percent of its selections, compared with 16 percent for the point-estimate rule under the same gain ranking, and abstains in about a quarter of replications. Omitted spillovers can invalidate the protection. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/esguard-4D2E/.

papers.title: Robust Log-Contrast Regression for High-Dimensional Compositional Microbiome Data with Outliers
papers.abstract: It is well known that microbiome sequencing data are naturally compositional and often have a complex subcomposition structure, as well as a lot of noise and some outliers. These characteristics make classical log-contrast regression difficult to apply, because it is sensitive to extreme values and cannot fully meet the linear constraints of compositional predictors. To tackle these issues, in this paper, we propose a robust log-contrast regression framework that incorporates the Huber loss function along with a Lasso penalty, which not only boosts resistance to outliers but also facilitates sparse variable selection. It is important to note that the general linear constraints, which are explicitly imposed, serve to preserve the algebraic coherence of compositional and subcompositional covariates. Under some mild assumptions, we theoretically prove that the proposed method achieves non-asymptotic guarantees in finite samples, comparable to those of Huber loss estimators, ensuring robustness. To implement the method efficiently, we develop a symmetric Gauss--Seidel-based alternating direction method of multipliers based on its dual formulation with a convergence guarantee, and it is also easy to implement in the sense that each subproblem admits a closed-form solution. To evaluate the statistical performance of the proposed method, we conduct a series of numerical experiments using simulated data and gut microbiome data, which show that the proposed method achieves better estimation accuracy, competitive prediction performance, and more reliable outlier identification than the benchmark method RobRegCC.

papers.title: Coupled unbiased MCMC for estimating Shapley effects under dependent inputs
papers.abstract: In global sensitivity analysis, Shapley effects provide a game-theoretic allocation of output variance among potentially dependent inputs. Their computation typically requires repeated conditional sampling, which can be challenging even when independent samples from the joint input distribution can be generated exactly. This difficulty arises naturally in hierarchical models, where conditioning on arbitrary subsets need not follow the generative order. To efficiently estimate Shapley effects under such dependence between input variables, we propose a permutation-based framework using coupled unbiased Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). Our proposed method combines two complementary coupling mechanisms: (i) a joint coupling of conditional distributions along a random permutation, designed to reduce the variance of estimated marginal contributions, and (ii) a meeting-based coupling of Markov chains that removes finite-time MCMC bias through a telescoping correction. Under suitable conditions, we prove that the resulting estimators for the unnormalized Shapley effects are unbiased, and have finite variance and finite expected computational cost. Numerical experiments with various test cases illustrate the computational efficiency of the proposed method.

papers.title: Time-Varying Quantile VAR Models: Estimation and Inference
papers.abstract: We study time-varying quantile VAR models in which the conditional quantile does not propagate linearly through the recursion, and develop a toolkit for impulse response analysis, which to the best of our knowledge has not been established elsewhere. For example, we establish Bahadur representation for quantile VAR regression, infer model parameters via smoothed check function, and define and investigate the best linear projection of the time-varying tau-quantile impulse response via local projections. An application to U.S. industrial production growth and credit spreads from 1919-2025 uncovers structural shifts in tail relationships, demonstrating downside asymmetry diminishes at longer forecast horizons.

papers.title: The uneven rise of AI-generated web content
papers.abstract: In less than five years, generative artificial intelligence (AI) has dramatically reshaped the public-facing web. Using a sample of more than 5 million crawlable webpages, we demonstrate that the share containing AI-generated text has increased precipitously, but unevenly. Our analyses reveal substantial differences in AI composition across language and domain categories (e.g., .edu, .com, or .gov). A higher fraction of English-language webpages contain AI-generated text compared to pages in other languages, and prevalence is substantially lower on .gov and .edu domains compared to .com. These distinctions persist even after accounting for compositional effects. We also find heterogeneity based on a page's position in the connectivity structure of the web. AI-generated text is most common and has increased most rapidly in pages that are the least central in the graph, which drives much of the overall growth in AI-generated text. A slower increase has taken place for more central pages, with the most central tier emerging as the least likely to contain AI-generated text. Methodologically, we use multiple AI detection tools, and generate estimates using a Bayesian hierarchical model that incorporates corrections for the detectors' statistical properties (both false positives and false negatives) and allows for different detector performance across groups, while propagating uncertainty in detector error rates into prevalence estimates. Our work suggests that AI is a prominent, but varied, contributor to public information and internet-based communication.

papers.title: Balanced State Subspaces for Mamba-2 State Compression
papers.abstract: Mamba-2 compresses all context into a fixed-size recurrent state that dominates decoding memory and bandwidth. Existing compressors quantize state values or prune state coordinates, scoring each channel independently in the native basis. We examine trained Mamba-2 states and find that energy is almost rank-one, but the output does not read the energetic directions: energy concentrates in a bias-like direction accumulated by the recurrence, while the content the output reads lives in a low-dimensional subspace that is not aligned with the state's coordinates. Even output-aware scores are computed coordinate by coordinate, so they miss the directions that determine the input--output map. Compression should therefore target the write--read subspace rather than individual coordinates. We propose \method{}, a post-training transform that instantiates balanced truncation with full controllability and observability Gramians and applies the rotation exactly via Mamba-2's scalar-identity transition. Because the useful rank varies widely across layers, we further introduce HARP, which allocates ranks per layer from the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers, improving both perplexity and retrieval over uniform budgets. Calibration takes a single forward pass, an order of magnitude faster than GHOST's released protocol, with lower peak memory. With HARP, \method{} halves the state dimension at an average WikiText-2 perplexity increase of $0.3$ points ($1.8\%$) across 130M--2.7B, versus $1.6$ ($9.3\%$) for GHOST, and the gap widens at 25\% retention.

papers.title: When Scatter Plots Hide the Data: Diagnosing Ties and Choosing the Right Display in R
papers.abstract: Scatter plots draw one mark per observation, so observations that share a location are hidden. In a two-item Likert survey of 2,757 respondents, 98.7% of the data lie under other points and the plot shows only 36 dots. The density-distribution sunflower plot of Dupont and Plummer addresses this by drawing raw points in sparse regions and sunflowers, whose petals count observations, in dense ones. It is not available in R, and its single petal weight for dense cells fails when cell counts span more than an order of magnitude: small dense cells collapse to one petal, and the count a reader decodes can be wrong by 150% or more. We propose geometric petal tiers, in which each cell uses the smallest weight among 1, b, b2, . . . observations per petal that keeps its flower within P petals. Every flower then has between about P/b and P petals, and the relative error of every decoded count is below b/(2P), 17.9% at the defaults b = 5 and P = 14. We also define tie diagnostics and decision rules that use them to choose between an ordinary scatter plot, jitter or transparency, a classic sunflower plot and geometric tiers. Both are implemented in the ggplot2 extension ggsunflower. We illustrate the methods on survey, automotive, historical and large commercial data, and in a simulation over 35 conditions geometric tiers keep the worst-cell error at or below 14% where a single weight reaches a median of 251%.

papers.title: Effect-Size Estimation and Confounding-Aware Permutations for PERMANOVA
papers.abstract: Motivation: PERMANOVA is widely used to test associations between covariates and high-dimensional data with arbitrary distributions, such as ecology, metabolomics, or microbial community profiling. In these contexts, its effect size measure (R2) is generally used to indicate how much the high-dimensional measurement covaries with respect to a separate, univariate measure. However, as we show, this conventional effect size is inflated under the null, resulting in values that do not accurately reflect the conventional expectation of "variance explained." Furthermore, standard permutation schemes yield inflated false positives in the presence of non-independent samples, such as repeated measure designs. Results: We introduce confounding-aware permutation schemes for both invariant and variant covariates. We additionally develop a causally-grounded, distance-based effect-size estimator derived from the Hájek average treatment effect estimator, providing interpretable effect sizes in the units of the chosen dissimilarity metric. Simulations using microbiome profiles demonstrate that these approaches control false positives while maintaining power, outperforming standard PERMANOVA implementations. Availability and Implementation: An R implementation is freely available in the permaBrioche module of the bioBakery ecosystem https://huttenhower.sph.harvard.edu/permabrioche. Contact: chuttenh@hsph.harvard.edu

papers.title: Two-sample inference for sequence-derived feature distributions from deep sequencing data
papers.abstract: Many biological contexts involve heterogeneous populations of related molecular variants within a single individual. For example, some viral infections such as HIV-1 exhibit substantial diversity within a single host. Advances in sequencing technology now make it possible to characterize such populations by generating up to thousands of genetic sequences from a biological sample. In many settings, each sequence can be mapped to a numeric feature, such as Hamming distance to a reference sequence. This collection of feature values defines a one-dimensional distribution that characterizes individual-level viral diversity. When comparing these features across independent groups, past analyses have typically reduced each individual's data to a single summary value, such as the mean or mode. We propose a framework that retains the full individual-level distribution as the object of analysis. Drawing on existing tools from distributional data analysis, our framework uses Wasserstein barycenters to summarize the observed individual-level distributions within groups into a single representative distribution. These group barycenters are then compared using differences in quantiles and tested for equality. A practical challenge is that the number of sequences obtained, known as sequencing depth, can vary across biological samples. Through simulation studies, we examine when low sequencing depth can distort inference and present practical strategies for addressing these issues. We then illustrate the framework using data from the HIV-1 Antibody Mediated Prevention efficacy trials and a human B cell receptor sequencing study of vaccine-elicited immune responses. By using the entire collection of sequences for each individual, our approach can reveal group differences that may be obscured by single-number summary analyses.

papers.title: Uniform Strong Convergence of Kernel-Type Estimators for m-LENQD Sequences with Applications
papers.abstract: In this paper, we firs tderiv eth eunifor mstron gconsistenc yan dth ecorrespondin gconvergence rates for kernel estimators of both the distribution function and the probability density function for sequences of m-linearly extended negative quadrant dependent (m-LENQD) random variables under mild regularity conditions. The obtained results significantl yimprov ean dexten dexisting ones in the literature. As their theoretical applications, we further establish the uniform strong consistency and convergence rates for estimators of the hazard rate function and the mode of the density function. Numerical simulations and a real data analysis are conducted to assess the finite- sample performance of the proposed estimators, confirmin gth easymptoti cpropertie sderive din the theoretical analysis.

papers.title: Stationary Action Principles for Neuronal Growth
papers.abstract: Neuronal growth is guided by biochemical, mechanical, and geometrical cues while being influenced by stochastic fluctuations in cytoskeletal dynamics, adhesion, and growth cone sensing. Here, we develop two complementary variational descriptions of mechanically guided axonal growth. First, for neurons growing on periodic parallel micropatterns, we use Langevin and Fokker--Planck models to derive a stochastic path action incorporating deterministic substrate guidance and random fluctuations. The probability of a growth trajectory decreases exponentially with this action, and the most probable trajectories correspond to minimum action paths for fixed boundary conditions. Second, for axons growing on substrates with spatially varying stiffness, we show that stiffness dependent traction generates mechanical guidance and axonal turning at stiffness interfaces. In the quasi-static limit, this response leads to a Fermat-like spatial action with an effective axonal refractive index determined by the traction and substrate stiffness relationship. The resulting framework predicts axonal refraction across stiffness boundaries, including an approximate Snell-like relation and a critical angle condition. Although the stochastic and Fermat-like actions have distinct physical meanings and ranges of validity, both describe how substrate mechanics constrain axonal trajectories. These results connect measurable quantities, including drift, diffusion, stiffness, traction, and growth direction, to global properties of axonal paths and provide a framework for designing biomimetic substrates for controlled neuronal growth and regeneration.

papers.title: Mirror Likelihood for Modeling Manifold Data with Application on Correlation Time Series
papers.abstract: Manifold-valued data arise in a wide range of scientific applications. Existing statistical methods typically follow either an intrinsic approach, which characterizes the manifold itself via quantities such as geodesic distance or the Fréchet mean, or an extrinsic approach, which embeds the manifold into an ambient Euclidean space, performs unconstrained statistical estimation, and projects the result back to the manifold. While the latter is conceptually and computationally simple, likelihood-based extrinsic solutions remain scarce, due to the lack of a general recipe for choosing an embedding map and for characterizing its impact on the transformed distribution. In this article, we tackle the problem using an augmented likelihood approach: we view the manifold-valued data as the Fenchel mirror map of a latent variable, which is nearly unconstrained, and model the latent variable with a canonical distribution, such as Gaussian. The key transform, the Fenchel mirror map, is a generalization of the Euclidean projection and can effectively map into the interior of the manifold. Taking a Bayesian approach, the proposed framework enjoys a generative model interpretation and an augmented likelihood free from intractable normalization constants, and it supports principled uncertainty quantification and flexible model-based extensions. We study the theoretical and computational properties of the framework and demonstrate its utility in analyzing neuroimaging data of high-dimensional correlation time series, where each correlation matrix is rank deficient.

papers.title: Bias Correction and Inference for Panel Quantile Regression
papers.abstract: We develop a large-$n$, large-$T$ theory for the unsmoothed fixed-effects quantile regression estimator, paralleling Hahn and Newey (2004) for smooth nonlinear panel models. An exact rank-score identity for the profiled criterion, with a convexity argument, delivers the leading incidental parameter bias of the slope estimator, of order $T^{-1}$, in closed form. When $n$ and $T$ grow at the same rate, the estimator is asymptotically normal but in general not centred, and conventional intervals are invalid. Admissible growth of $n$ relative to $T$, up to $n=o(T^3)$, depends on the regularity of the conditional error densities. A split-panel jackknife removes the leading bias throughout this range and yields valid inference. In serially dependent panels whose dependence decays geometrically or polynomially, the bias acquires a term from the dependence between regressors and errors of different periods, the jackknife remains valid with contiguous but not with interleaved half-panels, and clustered standard errors are valid.

papers.title: Fixed-Horizon Error Rates for Array-RQMC Metropolis-Hastings
papers.abstract: This paper studies randomised quasi-Monte Carlo (RQMC) methods for Metropolis--Hastings (MH) algorithms, whose accept--reject discontinuity complicates RQMC analysis. To circumvent some of these complications, we study Array-RQMC for MH, with $N$ replicated chains evolved over a fixed time horizon $T$, where we make use of Hilbert sorting for joint multidimensional updates at each step. For one-dimensional MH and bounded-variation test functions, we prove a sampling mean squared error bound of $\mathcal O_T(N^{-4/3})$ relative to the finite-horizon expectation. For product targets, coordinatewise Array-RQMC Metropolis-within-Gibbs retains this exponent for additive marginal bounded-variation tests, with constants that may depend on dimension. With Gaussian random-walk proposals, the bounds extend to scalar and additive marginal polynomials with an additional factor $(\log N)^\ell$, where $\ell$ is the maximum polynomial degree. For joint updates in state dimension $p$ using $p$ proposal uniforms, we provide a conditional $\mathcal O_T(N^{-1-1/(p+2)})$ framework under regularity assumptions that are not verified for the joint multidimensional examples. Numerical experiments support the verified one-dimensional theory and demonstrate variance reduction for joint Hilbert-sorted updates, including Bayesian logistic regression, while illustrating the limitations of these gains as dimension increases.

papers.title: Finite-population inference for cross-fitted estimators of treatment contrasts in stratified multistage surveys
papers.abstract: Health surveys often sample clusters within strata and then individuals within clusters, and flexible outcome and treatment models complicate inference for adjusted contrasts from such surveys. We establish finite-population limit theory for survey-weighted augmented inverse-probability-weighted estimation within the double machine learning framework, using cross-fitting that keeps whole clusters together; a cross-fitted targeted maximum likelihood estimator inherits the results under additional targeting conditions. With first-stage clusters drawn by simple random sampling without replacement within strata, the theory allows arbitrary within-cluster dependence, appreciable sampling fractions, and many small strata, a few large strata, or both. Under bounded cluster sizes, a cluster-generation model and nuisance convergence-rate conditions, the estimator is asymptotically normal about the finite-population contrast, and a stability property derived from the cluster model controls the cross-fitting error without entropy conditions. The stratified ultimate-cluster variance estimator, without a first-stage finite-population correction, consistently estimates a with-replacement variance that is at least the without-replacement design variance of the normal limit, so the resulting intervals are asymptotically conservative, and exact when the excess is negligible. In simulations, near-nominal or higher coverage coexisted, in different settings, with remainder diagnostics above the study's negligibility benchmark and with inaccurate standard errors. In three Service Provision Assessment surveys from Malawi and Haiti, each frame treated as a fixed population and resampled 500 times, mean reported standard errors were 4%-20% larger than the empirical standard deviations, while coverage of whole-frame reference values was near or above nominal.

papers.title: Many Hands Make Light Work: Long-Term Effect Inference for the Experiment Reservoir
papers.abstract: The surrogate index method is the modern standard for estimation of long-term effects in a designed experiment using only short-term outcomes. This method relies on the surrogacy and comparability assumptions which may be violated in practice leading to estimation bias. We propose a new method called Experiment Reservoir Surrogate (ERS) which leverages a reservoir of historical long-term experiments that is common in large-scale experimentation platforms. ERS avoids the surrogacy assumption by predicting the long-term average treatment effect directly, and relaxes the comparability assumption by matching to similar historical experiments, without requiring every experiment in the reservoir to be comparable to the target experiment. Moreover, ERS is memory-efficient, as it only requires aggregate data for each time period, instead of raw individual-level data. We theoretically justify the improved efficiency of ERS and demonstrate the improvement empirically on a reservoir of experiments from the online platform DoorDash.

papers.title: Estimating the Effect of a Low Nicotine Standard on Smoking Behavior in the U.S. Population
papers.abstract: In January of 2025, the FDA announced a proposed rule to set a nationwide nicotine standard of 0.7 mg/cigarette that would reduce nicotine levels in cigarettes by 95$\%$. Past trials comparing very-low nicotine content (VLNC) cigarettes and normal nicotine content (NNC) cigarettes consistently found randomization to receive VLNC cigarettes reduces cigarette consumption. However, these results are not intrinsically generalizable, as the trials exhibited partial treatment non-adherence and were not designed as representative samples of the United States (U.S.) population of people who smoke (PWS). Existing transportability methods do not account for non-adherence or target a different estimand. Additionally, non-adherence cannot be directly observed and must be estimated using biomarkers of nicotine exposure, and different biomarkers were collected across trials. To estimate the effect of full adherence to a low nicotine standard in the U.S. population of PWS, we develop a novel inverse odds weighting estimator for transporting an intervention's effect to a fully adherent target population, and propose a bivariate mixture model approach for estimating adherence using biomarkers that allows partial missingness in one of the biomarkers. Finally, we use our method to transport inferences from seven trials investigating VLNC cigarettes to a representative sample of U.S. PWS.

papers.title: Contextual Factors Behind Income Inequality: A Predictive Analysis
papers.abstract: Income inequality remains a central concern in economics and public policy, yet conclusions about its predictors often depend on both the factors considered and the measure of inequality used. This paper examines the predictive importance of a broad set of indicators covering structural factors, capital structure, financial-sector development, political institutions, regional classification, human capital, globalization, and technology. Using data for 88 countries from 1970 to 2017 and six inequality measures from the World Income Inequality Database (WIID), we apply a machine learning approach to assess the relative predictive importance of 35 candidate indicators across alternative income inequality measures. The analysis proceeds in three stages: a full specification including all candidate indicators, a category-representative specification with one common indicator from each conceptual category, and an inequality-specific specification allowing the most predictive indicator within each category to vary across inequality measures. Regional classification is the dominant predictor across all specifications and inequality measures, although its broad nature prevents identification of the specific regional characteristics underlying this result. Political and technology indicators provide the most consistent additional predictive information, whereas the importance of human capital, financial development, and globalization varies across inequality measures. Technology is particularly informative for top-income concentration, while returns to capital are more relevant for measures capturing gaps between the upper and lower parts of the income distribution.

papers.title: Directional Statistics on Circles and Spheres: A New Angle on Data
papers.abstract: Two compass bearings near north can have an ordinary arithmetic mean pointing south: the difficulty is that angles live on a circle, not a straight line. Using real wind observations, diffusion-MRI orientations, and geometric examples from machine learning, this article introduces circular and axial averages, directional variability, and probability models on circles and spheres. The guiding principle is to identify the geometry and symmetries of the observations before choosing a statistical method.

papers.title: Structure, Not Sequence: Tracking and Validating Folding Mechanisms in ESMFold's Trunk with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Structure predictors like ESMFold fold proteins using neural network computation and have transformed structural biology. However, the driving mechanism from amino-acid (AA) sequence to 3D structure is insufficiently understood, and biological meaning remains locked in the dense network. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promising results in obtaining interpretable concept features over an overcomplete basis of intermediate protein sequence-model representations. Yet folding models, which predict physical shape from AA sequence semantics, have no such account. We hypothesize that the features carrying the folding computation evolve in the 3D structural regression process. In this paper, we interpret the folding trunk in three steps. First, a pilot analysis on the representation distribution across modules and recycles locates distinct spatial computation in the trunk. Second, the dictionaries expose a division of labor: the single representation carries inherited semantics, and the pair representation computes the pairwise geometry. Third, we interpret the dictionary at scale with a reasoning language model, trace how the concepts compose across blocks by gradient-based attribution, and follow the interpreted code to the model's folding output, verifying where the computation aligns with, or departs from, known biochemistry. Together, the sparse dictionaries we train capture the relational geometry the trunk computes beyond the sequence model, and their concept activations forecast the model's own fold quality, turning the black-box folding trunk into a sparse, interpretable, and scientifically verifiable circuit.

papers.title: Relaxed MEMs: Enhancing Borrowing in Multisource Exchangeability Models for Small Sample Applications
papers.abstract: Information sharing in clinical trials provides a promising way to increase trial efficiency, specifically in rare disease settings where sample sizes are small. Multisource Exchangeability Modeling (MEM) is a method that incorporates historical data from potentially multiple data sources, such as past trials, by exploring all possible configurations of exchangeability and provides a weight estimate for each configuration, allowing the user to quantify how much is being borrowed from each source. While MEMs have previously been shown to be asymptotically consistent, small sample sizes introduce uncertainty that naturally limits the amount of borrowing MEMs can facilitate. The proposed ``relaxed MEMs'' provide a mathematical framework for relaxing or removing those limits and allowing greater borrowing even in small-sample settings. Several relaxed MEM versions are proposed, and all strategies provide enhanced borrowing with minimal sacrifice in the bias and variance of the mean estimates. Specifically, the maximum absolute mean bias was 3.5\% (0.035) of the true mean in the two source continuous outcome settings and 6.4\% (0.032) of the true proportion in the two source binary outcome settings (absolute mean bias was 1.4\% (0.014) and 3.6\% (0.018), respectively, for traditional MEMs) and variance decreased relative to traditional MEMs across all exchangeable and small difference scenarios. The methods were then demonstrated using two endpoints from a series of phase II trials in cystic fibrosis.

papers.title: Indirect inference in incomplete and partially identified econometric models
papers.abstract: We extend the indirect inference principle to structural econometric models that are incomplete, in the sense that a single value of the structural parameter may be compatible with multiple distributions of the observed endogenous variables, so that the structural parameter is typically only partially identified. We define the binding function as the smallest norm of the auxiliary estimating equations over the set of data generating processes compatible with the structural model. Hence, we obtain a confidence region by inverting a test of the hypothesis that the binding function vanishes at the pseudo-true value. A dual characterization based on random set theory makes the binding function computationally tractable. We define the auxiliary model conditionally on the covariates to remove its dependence on the unknown covariate distribution and we show that the binding function is Lipschitz and Hadamard directionally differentiable, so that the numerical delta method delivers valid critical values. We show that the method provides significant computational advantages without relinquishing informativeness in a simulation experiment based on an entry game with 100 potential entrants.

papers.title: Probabilistic Causal Panel Analysis
papers.abstract: Many causal panel estimators construct counterfactuals using weights or latent structure estimated directly from observed outcomes, making treatment-effect estimates sensitive to observation noise. Bayesian hierarchical models can account for this noise and borrow information across related observations, but existing Bayesian approaches to causal panel analysis generally combine outcome modeling and counterfactual imputation in estimator-specific formulations that can require bespoke sampling algorithms. We develop a framework that learns the latent untreated panel with a probabilistic model and applies established causal estimators to its posterior draws. The model accommodates non-Gaussian observations and structured pooling, while re-estimation across draws propagates uncertainty through counterfactual imputation. We establish conditions for posterior consistency of counterfactual imputation, characterize how pooling affects imputation risk, and develop fast cross-validation for model selection and calibration of predictive uncertainty for treatment effects. Our results show that probabilistic modeling can improve counterfactual imputation, particularly when observation noise is substantial and the pooling structure is informative.

papers.title: Close Races and Similarity Bias: A Bayesian Analysis of the Ranked Ballots for the Ballon d'Or
papers.abstract: The Ballon d'Or ranks players whose contributions have no common unit, so its results are often disputed. Regressions of award points describe associations but not how complete ballots arise or how likely a different winner would be. We propose a Bayesian mixture-of-experts model for partial rankings that learns nonlinear performance relationships, the number of voting styles and journalists' style memberships. A shared soft regression tree with style-specific leaf values lets styles evaluate the same season records differently on a common basis. Region-dependent mixing probabilities and journalist--nominee similarity terms separate geographic differences in voting styles from affinity within a style, and journalist- and rank-specific precisions capture remaining variation. We establish identification and consistency for the number of occupied styles under explicit conditions; simulations examine recovery, calibration and robustness to misspecification. Applied to all 176 published ballots from 2019 and 99 from 2024, the model compares award outcomes under changes in affinity and jury composition. For 2019, Messi's probability of winning with a new jury from the same countries rises from 0.49 to 0.76 when similarity terms are removed. For 2024, the direction of this change depends on whether affinities differ by region. Regional representation changes winner probabilities more than jury size.

papers.title: Testing strong exogeneity in proxy SVARs with internal synthetic proxies
papers.abstract: Proxy SVARs often rely on a single credible proxy, leaving proxy exogeneity untestable. Narrative arguments used to justify proxy validity imply a stronger form of exogeneity. We formalize the strong exogeneity assumption and propose a corresponding test based on internal synthetic proxies. The approach uses the external proxy to locate the target-shock direction in the reduced-form innovations and synthesize the candidate shock into an additional internal synthetic proxies, which allows to test the joint exogeneity of the original and internal synthetic proxy. We derive the large-sample theory for the ISP test and show that the identification strength is governed by a direct measure of the target shock's non-Gaussianity. We study weak identification under asymptotic Gaussianity and develop an identification-robust version of the test. Monte Carlo experiments demonstrate the favorable power of the test when the proxy has a low signal-to-noise ratio. Applications to monetary policy and oil supply news shocks find no evidence against the exogeneity of the benchmark proxies.

papers.title: Not Just Why, but When and for Whom: Revisiting Common Estimands in Causal Inference
papers.abstract: Causal inference commonly defines an individual treatment effect as a quantity that varies across units. But we know such effects, even for a fixed unit, can also vary over time, across repeated studies, or over different methods of measurement, and they can even exhibit inherent stochasticity. In this work, we consider how such additional sources of variation create a need for more general notions of average treatment effects, including some estimands that have yet to be more formally explored by the causal inference community. This perspective also motivates a reconceptualization of our most common existing estimands, such as conditional average, sample average, and individual treatment effects (CATEs, SATEs, and ITEs), as subject to more axes of variation than are typically considered. We explore two main consequences of this reframing in the case where we have data from a single randomized controlled trial: (1) decision making in fixed samples and (2) uncertainty quantification during estimation. We find that different estimands, even for the same unit or the same sample, can qualitatively disagree on whether an effect is positive or negative. We demonstrate these issues empirically through a case study with real data and characterize through a simulation study how our assumptions about these sources of variation, even if we cannot observe the variation, can be consequential for estimation and proper coverage performance. Importantly, these phenomena arise even in the simplest of cases, where all structural and parametric assumptions are satisfied. More broadly, this paper aims to provide a preliminary investigation into an underexplored class of assumptions --- assumptions about unobserved non-confounders --- that should be considered when estimating treatment effects.

papers.title: Optimal tradeoffs between variance and sensitivity, via Hellinger-Kantorovich geometry
papers.abstract: While the goal of classical statistical theory is to minimize the variance of unbiased estimators, an additional goal of some recent research is to minimize or constrain other notions of the instability of estimators. In particular, a subset of the authors recently introduced a notion of instability termed "sensitivity", which represents the expected amount that an estimator would change if its inputs were infinitesimally perturbed. In this work, we study the multiobjective problem of minimizing both the variance and sensitivity over unbiased estimators in a given statistical model, and we aim to determine Pareto optimal tradeoffs between these two objectives. Our main results show that the Pareto front for these tradeoffs is precisely determined by endowing the statistical model with the Hellinger-Kantorovich geometry, which interpolates between the Hellinger and Wasserstein geometries that are known to be associated, respectively, with the separate minimization of variance and sensitivity. We also develop a $Z$-estimation technique which constructs estimators that asymptotically achieve Pareto optimal pairs of variance and sensitivity. While computing the Pareto front and constructing the resulting estimators in practice requires solving a continuum of partial differential equations, we fully execute this program in some parametric examples of interest where the analysis is already non-trivial. Our results also shed light on some classical statistical problems, for example by showing that the maximum likelihood estimator achieves the smallest asymptotic sensitivity among all estimators achieving the optimal asymptotic variance.

papers.title: Adequacy radii for stepped-wedge trials with time-varying effects
papers.abstract: Complete stepped-wedge designs guarantee eventual intervention delivery, but their final periods contain no concurrent controls. Under exposure-time heterogeneity this creates a design-analysis tension: a constant-effect analysis can be precise while targeting a design-dependent contrast, whereas an exposure-time indicator (ETI) analysis targets a prespecified time-averaged effect but may be much less precise. We develop an adequacy radius that quantifies the size of exposure-time heterogeneity compatible with a prespecified tolerance for estimand mismatch, and combine it with precision calculations to compare complete wedges with rollout-constrained hybrid designs that retain a wait-list arm. For a balanced wedge with a wait-list under the Hussey-Hughes model, the wait-list share and the correlation act on the constant-effect GLS estimand through a single scalar; we prove that the radius increases strictly with the wait-list share and decreases strictly with the within-cluster correlation, but remains bounded. Numerical optimisation and a model-based redesign of a weekend allied-health trial show that intermediate hybrids make estimand-aligned ETI analysis materially more affordable, giving a robustness-precision frontier rather than a binary choice between a complete wedge and a parallel trial. A second trial, of digital adherence support for tuberculosis treatment, has the same radius but no detectable heterogeneity; its test of a constant effect would detect heterogeneity large enough to halve the coverage of the nominal interval only 37% of the time. The contribution is a diagnostic and design principle: when exposure-time heterogeneity is plausible, retaining concurrent controls reduces the price of analysing the estimand one intends to report.
